subtitle: What companies and governments spend on AI, 2024 to 2026: capex, forecasts, enterprise budgets, power and public money, each figure dated and rated
at_a_glance: Gartner forecast on 16 September 2026 that worldwide AI spending will reach about $2.67 trillion in 2026, up 49.5% on its estimate of $1.79 trillion for 2025, with AI infrastructure about 56% of the total.

Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon and Meta spent about $508 billion on capital expenditure from January to September 2026, more than the roughly $413 billion they spent in all of 2025, according to Report AI's sum of their reported results.
The same four companies' full-year 2026 capex guidance, as given in late October 2026, adds up to roughly $720–740 billion, against about $245 billion of capex in calendar 2024.
IDC counted $318.7 billion of worldwide AI infrastructure spending in 2025, up 107% from $153.9 billion in 2024, and on 6 November 2026 raised its 2026 forecast to $521 billion.

Menlo Ventures estimated that US enterprises spent $37 billion on generative AI in 2025; its November 2026 report puts enterprise AI deployment spending at an annualised $176.8 billion in September 2026, on a new definition that is not comparable.
Anthropic's share of US enterprise LLM API spending rose from 24% in 2024 to 40% in 2025 and 55% in 2026, according to Menlo Ventures, an Anthropic investor.

Government AI money remains small next to corporate capex: the largest verified public items in 2026 are one-off vehicles such as Abu Dhabi's $49 billion MGX fund (July 2026) and the UK's £500 million Sovereign AI Fund (April 2026), not annual budgets.

chapters.action_title: Forecasters raised their 2026 AI spending estimates all year, and most of the new money is going to hardware
paras: Gartner forecast on 16 September 2026 that worldwide AI spending will reach about $2.67 trillion in 2026, up 49.5% on its estimate of about $1.79 trillion for 2025. It was the third time in eight months that Gartner raised its figure for the year: the January edition said $2.52 trillion and the May edition $2.59 trillion. Gartner expects a further rise to about $3.64 trillion in 2027. Its total is broad. It counts AI infrastructure, software, services, AI models, security and AI-enabled consumer devices, so it is best read as a measure of all spending that has some AI content rather than spending on AI alone. Gartner's figures are built from vendor revenue and buyer surveys, and the company does not publish its full method. Treat the total as an order of magnitude and the direction of revision as the signal.

Infrastructure is the largest component and the main reason for the revisions. Gartner puts 2026 AI infrastructure spending at about $1.48 trillion, roughly 56% of its total. IDC, which counts only AI-optimised servers and storage, measured $153.9 billion of such spending in 2024 and $318.7 billion in 2025, a rise of 107%. On 6 November 2026 IDC raised its 2026 forecast to $521 billion, from $497 billion in July and $487 billion in April, citing higher component prices, demand for CPU-based systems and continued cloud-provider capex. IDC expects the series to pass $1 trillion in 2029. The infrastructure share matters because hardware is bought ahead of demand: servers and data centres are paid for before the services that run on them earn revenue, which is why infrastructure leads every other category in both firms' figures.

The quarterly data show why the forecasts moved. IDC counted about $90 billion of AI infrastructure spending in the fourth quarter of 2025 and $89.7 billion in the first quarter of 2026, a flat start to the year that IDC attributes to paused deployments. Spending then rose to $121.4 billion in the second quarter, up 53% year on year and about a third on the previous quarter. Servers made up 98% of the value. One strong quarter was enough to lift the full-year forecast by $24 billion. The quarterly line is the closest thing to a measured series in this report. It is still an estimate, built from vendor revenue rather than buyers' accounts, and IDC revises past quarters when vendors restate, so the latest edition should always be used.

Two cautions apply to the headline totals. First, Gartner's figures for completed years are estimates that it revises: its September 2025 forecast put 2025 at $1.48 trillion, its January 2026 table at $1.757 trillion and its September 2026 table at $1.79 trillion, partly because categories were added. A growth rate computed across editions is not a measured growth rate. Second, the IDC and Gartner totals measure different things and should never be added together or used to check one another. They agree on direction, not on size. For 2026 the safest statement is the range of forecasts and their direction: every published figure for the year was revised upward between January and November, and none was revised down. That pattern can change quickly if hardware deliveries slip.

sidebar.title: Why AI spending forecasts disagree
sidebar.body: Gartner's $2.67 trillion and IDC's $521 billion for 2026 are both correct on their own terms. Gartner counts any spending with AI content, including AI-enabled smartphones and PCs, software with AI features and AI services. IDC's tracker counts AI-optimised servers and storage only. IDC also publishes a separate, broader spending guide, whose 2029 figure of $1.3 trillion is often misquoted as 'agentic AI spending'. Before comparing two figures, check four things: which categories are included, whether the year is complete (an estimate) or still ahead (a forecast), which edition of the forecast is being quoted, and whether the figure is an annual total or an annualised run-rate.

chapters.action_title: The four largest spenders' capex roughly doubled in two years and now runs ahead of the cash their businesses generate
paras: Capital expenditure is the most concrete measure of AI spending because it is reported quarterly in audited accounts. By Report AI's sum of reported figures, Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon and Meta spent about $245 billion in calendar 2024 and about $413 billion in calendar 2025, an increase of roughly 69%. From January to September 2026 they spent about $508 billion, already more than in all of 2025. The third quarter of 2026 alone accounted for about $207 billion: Amazon $75.9 billion, Alphabet $51.4 billion, Microsoft $45.2 billion and Meta $34.91 billion. Quarterly capex for the four has risen steeply since 2024: the third-quarter figure for 2026 alone was more than four-fifths of their combined spending for the whole of 2024.

Not all of this is AI. Capex also covers warehouses, offices, network equipment and conventional cloud capacity. But each company has said that the increase is driven by data centres, servers and accelerators for AI, and none breaks out an AI-only figure. The totals are also approximate because the companies use different bases: Amazon reports cash capex net of incentives, Microsoft and Meta include assets acquired under finance leases, and Alphabet reports purchases of property and equipment. Off-balance-sheet structures such as Meta's roughly $27 billion Hyperion financing with Blue Owl are not in these numbers at all. Analysts often call these totals 'AI capex'; it is more accurate to call them capex driven by AI, and to quote each company's own basis alongside each number.

Guidance points higher still. In late October 2026 Amazon reaffirmed about $220 billion for 2026, Alphabet held $195–205 billion, Meta narrowed its range to $135–145 billion and Microsoft gave about $170 billion, which most outlets read as calendar 2026 and one as its fiscal year to June 2027. Together that is roughly $720–740 billion, which implies about $220 billion in the fourth quarter. At the start of 2026 the same four had guided to roughly $630–650 billion. Alphabet and Amazon have said spending will rise again in 2027, without giving numbers. Guidance has moved in one direction: Alphabet's 2026 range rose from $175–185 billion in February to $180–190 billion in April and $195–205 billion in July, and Amazon's from about $200 billion to about $220 billion.

Oracle, which reports fiscal years ending in May, shows the same pattern from a smaller base: gross capex of $21.2 billion in fiscal 2025, $55.7 billion in fiscal 2026 and guidance of $90–95 billion for fiscal 2027, with $28.5 billion spent in its first quarter to August 2026. For Oracle, Meta, Alphabet and Amazon, capex now exceeds operating cash flow. Meta's free cash flow was negative $2.12 billion in the third quarter, Alphabet's about negative $9.1 billion and Amazon's negative $42.4 billion over twelve months. Between 26 October and 5 November 2026, Meta, Oracle and Alphabet raised more than $70 billion of new equity and debt. Oracle's new notes were priced at coupons of up to 8.65%. The cost of financing is now part of the cost of the build-out.

sidebar.title: How we count capex
sidebar.body: We use each company's reported capital expenditure for calendar years. Microsoft's fiscal year ends in June, so its calendar figures are sums of four fiscal quarters, marked DERIVED. Oracle's fiscal year ends in May and is shown separately. We use the basis each company reports and do not adjust for it: Amazon net of proceeds and incentives, Microsoft and Meta including finance leases, Alphabet purchases of property and equipment. Combined totals are therefore an order of magnitude, not a like-for-like sum. Guidance is shown as guidance and never on the same line as outcomes. Off-balance-sheet leases and joint ventures are excluded.

chapters.action_title: Electricity is the physical limit on AI spending, and data-centre demand is on course to double by 2030
paras: The International Energy Agency estimates that data centres worldwide used about 415 TWh of electricity in 2024, roughly 1.5% of global demand, and about 485 TWh in 2025. Sources differ on the 2025 growth rate, 17% in most secondary coverage against 'almost 20%' in IEA presentation material, so we rate it CONTESTED. The IEA's April 2026 update estimates that electricity used by AI-focused data centres rose about 50% in 2025, far faster than the total, and projects global data-centre consumption of about 950 TWh in 2030 in its base case, slightly above the 945 TWh in its 2025 edition. On those estimates, data centres would use a little under 3% of global electricity in 2030, against about 1.5% in 2024. The IEA says it will update its projections regularly.

There is no IEA estimate for 2026 yet. Gartner separately forecast in June 2026 that data-centre electricity demand will grow 26% in 2026. We do not apply Gartner's growth rate to the IEA's base because the two organisations measure differently. In the United States, where data centres are most concentrated, Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory projects data-centre electricity rising from 176 TWh in 2023 to between 325 and 580 TWh by 2028, a range wide enough to show how uncertain the build-out remains. The LBNL range runs from below to well above a doubling in five years. For spending, the important point is that grid connections, transformers and turbines take years to deliver, so electricity limits how fast capex can be turned into working capacity, whatever the budget.

Power shapes spending in two ways. It limits where capacity can be built, and it adds to the cost of each site. The 10-gigawatt project planned at a former uranium-enrichment plant in Ohio includes a 9.2-gigawatt gas-fired power station of its own, because no grid connection of that size is available; independent estimates put generation at about $37 billion of a roughly $500 billion total. Gas-turbine makers' order books stretch years ahead. These constraints help explain why IDC's first quarter of 2026 was flat and why some of Microsoft's third-quarter spending slipped. GE Vernova's gas-turbine backlog reached about 116 GW in the second quarter of 2026 against manufacturing capacity of roughly 20 GW a year. Money cannot buy delivery slots that do not exist.

The energy figures should be read with care. The IEA's numbers are modelled estimates, not metered totals, and the share attributable to AI rather than to conventional cloud and storage is itself an estimate. Per-query energy figures published by AI companies are small, about 0.2–0.3 watt-hours for a text prompt, but they exclude training and idle capacity. The fleet total is what matters for grids and spending, and it is the fleet total that is growing fastest. Water use follows the same pattern: per-site consumption depends on the cooling method, which announcements rarely specify. We therefore quote the IEA's fleet estimates, with their dates, and treat per-query figures as indicative. Neither tells us how much electricity goes to training models and how much to serving them.

sidebar.title: Estimates, projections and forecasts
sidebar.body: An estimate describes a year that has ended but has not been fully measured, such as the IEA's 485 TWh for 2025. A projection describes a scenario, such as the IEA's 950 TWh base case for 2030, which depends on stated assumptions about efficiency and demand. A forecast, such as Gartner's +26% for 2026, is a single expected outcome. We plot estimates and projections as separate series and never join them with a line. When an organisation revises an estimate, we keep both values and mark the later one RESTATED.

chapters.action_title: Enterprise spending on AI models is growing faster than adoption, and one provider now takes most of it
paras: Menlo Ventures' annual survey of US enterprise decision-makers is the most cited measure of company spending on generative AI. It estimated $37 billion of spending in 2025, 3.2 times its figure for 2024, split roughly evenly between applications (about $19 billion) and infrastructure (about $18 billion). Coding tools were the largest application category, at about $4 billion. Menlo's numbers have been restated as its method changed: it first reported $13.8 billion for 2024, then restated that to $11.5 billion after excluding inference. We keep both values. The survey covers about 500 US enterprise decision-makers combined with a bottom-up model of the market, so it describes large US buyers rather than all companies worldwide. Menlo invests in some of the companies whose revenue it estimates, which it discloses.

In November 2026 Menlo moved to a different measure: enterprise AI deployment spending as an annualised run-rate. It estimated that rate at $176.8 billion in September 2026, of which $99.5 billion was infrastructure and $77.3 billion applications, 5.4 times a restated $33 billion a year earlier. The figure excludes model training. It is not money spent in 2026 and it is not a successor to the $37 billion, so a growth rate from one to the other would be meaningless. SaaStr's reading of the report is that only 22% of the spending came out of software budgets. The run-rate is useful for one thing: it shows the level of spending at the end of the period, which is higher than the average across the year when spending is growing quickly.

The split by provider has changed faster than the totals. Menlo estimated that Anthropic took 24% of US enterprise LLM API spending in 2024, 40% in 2025 and 55% in 2026, while OpenAI went from 34% to 27% and then 31%. Google rose to 21% in 2025 and then fell to 9%. API spending itself ran at about $3.5 billion annualised in November 2024 and $8.4 billion by mid-2025; we found no dollar total for 2026. Menlo is an investor in Anthropic, and these are survey estimates, so we rate them MEDIUM. Together, Anthropic and OpenAI took 86% of enterprise API spending in 2026, up from 67% a year earlier; xAI and open-weight Chinese models together took just under 5%. Concentration rose even as the number of usable models grew.

Spending on AI agents is the most inflated category in public discussion. Gartner's widely quoted $206.5 billion for 2026 counts all spending on software that has agentic features built in, much of it existing enterprise applications. Its line for standalone AI agents and assistants is $29.2 billion for 2026, up from $16.5 billion in 2025. Research firms that size a standalone agents market put it at about $7–8 billion in 2025, with a median 2030 forecast of about $49 billion. Adoption data support the lower figures: Gartner's 2026 survey found 17% of organisations had deployed agents. McKinsey's 2025 survey found 23% of organisations scaling an agentic system somewhere and no more than 10% in any single function, and Gartner expects over 40% of agentic AI projects to be cancelled by the end of 2027.

sidebar.title: Why Menlo's figures cannot be chained
sidebar.body: Menlo Ventures has published four different bases in three years. Its November 2024 report gave $13.8 billion for 2024, including inference. Its December 2025 report gave $37 billion for 2025 and restated 2024 to $11.5 billion and 2023 to $1.7 billion, excluding inference. Its November 2026 report measures deployment spending as an annualised run-rate, $176.8 billion in September 2026 against a restated $33 billion a year earlier, excluding model training. Each figure is useful within its own edition. Growth rates should only be computed within one edition, and every quotation should name the edition and the measure.

chapters.action_title: AI is taking a growing share of technology spending, but industry rankings depend on what is measured
paras: Comparing Gartner's AI spending forecast with its own forecast of worldwide IT spending gives a rough measure of AI's weight in technology budgets. On our arithmetic, AI spending was about 19% of IT spending in 2024, about 32% in 2025 and is forecast at about 42% in 2026, when Gartner expects IT spending of $6.39 trillion. The ratio assumes that Gartner's AI categories sit inside its IT total, which Gartner does not state, and part of the rise reflects Gartner widening its AI definition. It describes market spending, not the budget of a typical company. The same calculation using Gartner's earlier editions would give different values, so the ratio should be quoted with its inputs and years. It is a rough indicator, not a statistic.

Surveys of buyers point in the same direction without giving a clean share. Futurum's September 2026 survey of 1,636 enterprise decision-makers found 46.9% reporting AI spending over budget in the second half of 2026, and 38.7% of those said they had moved money from elsewhere in the IT budget to cover it. RBC's December 2025 survey of 117 IT leaders found 90% planned to increase AI spending in 2026. Neither survey gives the share of IT budgets spent on AI. Both surveys suggest AI is being funded partly by moving money, not only by adding it. BCG's May 2026 survey of 423 IT leaders found they expected overall IT spending to grow 5.8% in 2026, far less than any AI spending series, and BCG reported that buyers were pulling back in other areas to pay for AI.

By industry, the ranking depends on the measure. On IDC's all-AI measure, banking was the largest spender worldwide in 2024, with about $31.3 billion and more than 20% of the total; banking, software and information services, and retail together accounted for about $89.6 billion. In Europe, IDC puts banking at 12.6% of AI spending in 2026 and financial services as a whole at 19.2%. IDC's worldwide industry tables for 2025 and 2026 are not public. IDC expects the top three verticals to reach about $222 billion by 2028. Financial services' weight reflects long-standing use of machine learning in fraud detection, credit scoring and trading as well as newer generative tools; JPMorgan alone has said it spends about $2 billion a year on AI within an $18 billion technology budget.

On Menlo's narrower measure of vertical generative-AI software, healthcare led in 2025 with $1.5 billion, 43% of about $3.5 billion, followed by legal at $650 million. The two rankings are not in conflict. Banks spend heavily across all forms of AI, including fraud detection and risk models built over many years, while healthcare providers are buying new generative tools, such as clinical documentation, faster than other sectors. Any statement that one industry 'spends the most on AI' should name the measure. Healthcare organisations' adoption of domain-specific AI tools reached 22% in 2025, about ten times the 2023 level, according to Menlo. 'Other verticals', including financial services, made up about $990 million. All of these sums are small beside capex.

sidebar.title: How we derived AI's share of IT spending
sidebar.body: Share = Gartner worldwide AI spending ÷ Gartner worldwide IT spending for the same year. 2024: $987.9 billion ÷ $5,114.8 billion = 19.3%, from the September 2025 AI table and the January 2025 IT table. 2025: $1,786.7 billion ÷ $5,581.7 billion = 32.0%, where 2025 IT spending is Gartner's 2026 total of $6,391 billion divided by its stated growth of 14.5%. 2026: $2,670.5 billion ÷ $6,391 billion = 41.8%. All inputs are Gartner's; the ratio is ours and is marked DERIVED. It is not a survey of company IT budgets.

chapters.action_title: Government AI spending is small next to corporate capex, and its biggest headlines are not budgets
paras: Public AI money is measured in single-digit billions a year where corporate capex is measured in hundreds of billions. The US requested $3.3 billion of non-defence federal AI research and development for fiscal 2025, up from $3.1 billion for fiscal 2024; we did not find the fiscal 2026 total. Defence is larger: the Pentagon's fiscal 2026 request included $13.4 billion for AI and autonomy. Brookings counted $7.2 billion of federal AI contract obligations in 2026 to May, almost all for the Department of Defense, though its 2024 base differs between accounts ($355 million or $675 million). These are budget requests and contract records, not outlays, and they use different definitions. GAO counted $5.6 billion of federal AI contract obligations over fiscal 2022–24 using another method, so neither series can be extended with the other.

Elsewhere the largest commitments are one-off vehicles. China registered the ¥344 billion (about $47.5 billion) semiconductor 'Big Fund III' in May 2024 and a ¥60.1 billion (about $8.2 billion) national AI fund in January 2025. The EU's verifiable public commitment is more than €2.7 billion for EuroHPC AI Factories over 2024–27; its €200 billion InvestAI is a mobilisation total that includes hoped-for private capital. The $500 billion Stargate venture contains no US federal funds. Both Chinese funds are equity vehicles registered once and invested over many years, not annual budgets. China also announced in March 2025 a national venture-capital guidance fund intended to mobilise about ¥1 trillion over 20 years. InvestAI includes a planned €20 billion public-private fund for AI gigafactories.

The UK set a £2 billion AI envelope for 2025–30 in its June 2025 Spending Review, about half for sovereign compute, launched a £500 million Sovereign AI Fund in April 2026 and added £60 million in the October 2026 Budget. Reports of a '£700 million sovereign AI fund' describe the Budget's wider AI package, whose size is reported as £600 million or £700 million. In the Gulf, Abu Dhabi's MGX closed a $49 billion first fund in July 2026, and Saudi Arabia's HUMAIN, launched in May 2025, has not disclosed its capital. MGX invests commercially for return and holds stakes in OpenAI, Anthropic and xAI, so it is better compared with a sovereign-wealth fund than with a budget. Its stated goal is more than $100 billion of assets.

These figures cannot be added together. An annual appropriation, a fund registered once and invested over years, a sovereign-wealth vehicle that invests for return and a mobilisation headline are four different things. By verifiable annual budget, Japan's ¥1.23 trillion (about $7.9 billion) for chips and AI in fiscal 2026 and South Korea's ₩10.1 trillion (about $7.4 billion) for 2025 remain larger than the US non-defence AI R&D line. None is close to a single quarter of one hyperscaler's capex. India's IndiaAI Mission, at about $1.25 billion from 2024, and Singapore's more than S$1 billion are smaller still. Governments shape where AI capacity is built through permits, power and export rules far more than through their own spending.

sidebar.title: Four kinds of public AI money
sidebar.body: Appropriation: money a legislature or ministry has allocated for a year, such as US federal AI R&D; the only kind that can be compared across countries. Equity vehicle: capital registered once and invested over years, such as China's national AI fund. Sovereign vehicle: public capital invested commercially for return, such as MGX or HUMAIN. Mobilisation headline: a total that bundles public money with private capital a government hopes to attract, such as InvestAI's €200 billion. We label every government figure by type and never sum across types.

comparison.action_title: Between 2024 and 2026 every measured AI spending series at least doubled, but the measures moved further apart
paras: On the measures that are counted rather than modelled, AI spending roughly doubled each year. Big-four capex went from about $245 billion in 2024 to about $413 billion in 2025, and reached about $508 billion in the first nine months of 2026. IDC's AI infrastructure series went from $153.9 billion to $318.7 billion, with $521 billion forecast for 2026. Enterprise API spending, enterprise generative-AI budgets and data-centre electricity all rose, though electricity grew far more slowly, by about 17–20% in 2025, because efficiency gains absorb part of the hardware growth.

Across companies, Amazon spent the most in each year, but Alphabet grew fastest: its January–September 2026 capex of $132.0 billion was 2.5 times its full-year 2024 figure. Microsoft's 2026 spending to September matched its whole 2025 total. Among model providers, Anthropic's share of enterprise API spending more than doubled from 2024 to 2026, while Google's rose and then fell. Meta's 2026 guidance is about twice its 2025 total, and Amazon's nine-month spending in 2026 exceeded every company's full-year figure for 2025.

The comparison also shows how unstable the measures are. Gartner's estimate for 2025 moved by more than $300 billion between editions, Menlo changed its definition twice, and IDC revised its 2026 infrastructure forecast three times. A reader comparing years should use one source and one edition at a time, and treat any cross-source growth rate as unreliable.

exhibits.title: On every measured series, AI spending roughly doubled between 2024 and 2025 and is on course to rise again in 2026
exhibits.subtitle: Key AI spending measures by year, with status of each figure
exhibits.source: Source: data/spending.json (Gartner, IDC, Menlo Ventures, IEA, company results); Report AI analysis
exhibits.notes: Big-four capex and AI share of IT spending are DERIVED. Gartner's 2024 and 2025 values come from different editions with different categories. Menlo's 2026 report uses an annualised run-rate ($176.8B) that is not a successor to the $37B. The 2026 column mixes year-to-date actuals and forecasts; read each cell's label.

outlook.action_title: In 2027 the question is whether spending keeps outrunning cash flow, and the first test is fourth-quarter capex
paras: Every forecast available in November 2026 expects AI spending to rise again in 2027: Gartner projects about $3.64 trillion of worldwide AI spending, IDC expects AI infrastructure to pass $1 trillion by 2029, and Alphabet and Amazon have said their capex will increase. The risk to that view is financial rather than technical. Three of the four largest spenders had negative free cash flow in the third quarter of 2026, and the gap is being filled with bonds, new shares and off-balance-sheet structures whose cost is rising, with some data-centre debt marketed at 11% or more.

Two things would change our view. A cut to 2027 capex plans by any of the four, or a first downward revision to Gartner's or IDC's forecasts, would signal that the build-out has peaked. Conversely, enterprise spending on models and agents growing fast enough to cover the depreciation on this capex would show the spending is being earned back; on current figures, measured enterprise revenue streams are an order of magnitude smaller than capex.

watch.signal: A full-year total below ~$700B would mean guidance was missed; first 2027 guidance below the 2026 level would mark a peak.

watch.now: Meta −$2.12B (Q3 2026), Alphabet ≈ −$9.1B (Q3 2026), Amazon −$42.4B (12 months to Sep 2026)
watch.signal: A second straight quarter of negative free cash flow at all three, with further equity raises, would make financing, not demand, the binding constraint.
A downward revision in the next edition would be the first of the cycle.
Two consecutive quarters of sequential decline would contradict the $521B full-year forecast.

An IEA estimate for 2026 above ~610 TWh (+26%, Gartner's forecast rate) would put grids, not chips, at the centre of 2027 spending plans.

definitions.def: Spending on long-lived assets such as data centres, servers and land, capitalised and depreciated over years. Reported quarterly by listed companies; each company uses its own basis.
Spending on AI-optimised servers and storage, measured by IDC's quarterly tracker from vendor revenue. Hardware only.
Gartner's total of spending on AI infrastructure, software, services, models, security and AI-enabled devices. Values for completed years are estimates that Gartner revises.
Menlo Ventures' survey-based estimate of US enterprise spending on generative-AI applications and infrastructure; definition has changed between editions.
Spending in a recent period scaled to a full year. Not the same as money spent in a calendar year.

definitions.term: Standalone AI agents vs agentic software
definitions.def: Standalone: products sold as AI agents or assistants. Agentic software: all software with agent features built in, including existing applications. Gartner's $29.2B and $206.5B for 2026 measure these two things.
Money a legislature or ministry has allocated for a period. Distinct from equity funds, sovereign-wealth vehicles and mobilisation headlines.
Terawatt-hour, one billion kilowatt-hours. Global electricity demand is roughly 30,000 TWh a year.

2024.action_title: In 2024 AI spending became an infrastructure story, and big-tech capex rose by about 60%
paras: Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon and Meta spent about $245 billion on capital expenditure in calendar 2024, by Report AI's sum of their reported figures, up from about $151 billion in 2023. Amazon spent about $77.7 billion on a net cash basis, Microsoft about $75.6 billion including finance leases, Alphabet $52.5 billion and Meta about $39.2 billion. IDC counted $153.9 billion of worldwide spending on AI-optimised servers and storage. Gartner later estimated total worldwide AI spending for the year at about $988 billion, on a broader definition that includes AI software, services and AI-enabled devices. The gap between the IDC and Gartner figures reflected what each counted, not a disagreement about the market. Sequoia's essay 'AI's $600B Question' (June 2024) framed the gap between this capex and AI revenue, and became the reference point for the debate that followed.

Enterprise budgets for generative AI were still small. Menlo Ventures reported in November 2024 that US enterprises spent $13.8 billion on generative AI in 2024, about six times its 2023 figure; in December 2025 it restated 2024 to $11.5 billion after excluding inference. Model API spending ran at about $3.5 billion a year by November. OpenAI held 34% of enterprise API spending and Anthropic 24%. Banking was the largest industry on IDC's all-AI measure, at about $31.3 billion. Applications accounted for $4.6 billion of Menlo's original total and large language models for $6.5 billion, so most enterprise generative-AI money still went to models. Banking, software and information services and retail together accounted for about $89.6 billion of AI spending on IDC's measure, about 38% of the total.

The physical cost became visible. The IEA estimates that data centres used about 415 TWh of electricity in 2024, about 1.5% of global demand. Public money was modest in comparison: the US requested about $3.1 billion of non-defence federal AI research for fiscal 2024, and China registered a ¥344 billion semiconductor fund in May. Most government commitments that year were one-off funds rather than recurring budgets. Electricity for AI-accelerated servers was growing about 30% a year against about 9% for conventional servers, the IEA estimated. Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory projected that US data-centre electricity could reach 325–580 TWh by 2028, from 176 TWh in 2023. India approved its IndiaAI Mission, about $1.25 billion, in March 2024, and the $52.7 billion US CHIPS and Science Act continued to underwrite the chip supply chain.

2025.action_title: In 2025 most AI spending measures roughly doubled, and enterprise money shifted between model providers
paras: Big-four capex rose to about $413 billion in calendar 2025, roughly 69% more than in 2024: Amazon about $131.8 billion, Microsoft about $118.0 billion, Alphabet $91.4 billion and Meta $72.2 billion. IDC counted $318.7 billion of AI infrastructure spending, up 107%, including about $90 billion in the fourth quarter alone. Gartner's estimate of worldwide AI spending for the year rose with each edition, from a $1.48 trillion forecast in September 2025 to about $1.79 trillion in its September 2026 table, partly because it added categories. Oracle's capex for its fiscal year to May 2026 reached about $55.7 billion. Alphabet's capex rose about 74% and Meta's about 84%, by our calculation from the reported figures, and Microsoft's fiscal year to June 2025 alone came to $88.7 billion. Each company ended the year guiding to more for 2026.

Enterprises spent about $37 billion on generative AI, according to Menlo Ventures, 3.2 times its restated 2024 figure, with coding tools the largest application at about $4 billion. API spending reached about $8.4 billion annualised by mid-year, and Anthropic overtook OpenAI, taking 40% of enterprise API spending against 27%. Gartner's later figures put spending on standalone AI agents and assistants at $16.5 billion in 2025 and on all software with agentic features at $86.4 billion. Menlo also estimated a $3.5 billion vertical generative-AI segment, led by healthcare at $1.5 billion. In June 2025 Gartner forecast that over 40% of agentic AI projects would be cancelled by the end of 2027, and McKinsey's November 2025 survey found 23% of organisations scaling an agentic system.

Data-centre electricity use rose to about 485 TWh, according to the IEA, with AI-focused sites up about 50%. Governments made large announcements but smaller commitments: the EU's €200 billion InvestAI was a mobilisation headline over a >€2.7 billion AI Factories programme, the $500 billion Stargate venture was private, China registered a ¥60.1 billion AI fund, the UK set a £2 billion envelope to 2030 and Saudi Arabia launched HUMAIN. The UK's envelope included about £1 billion for sovereign compute. In November 2025 the US authorised advanced chip exports to HUMAIN and G42, each cleared to buy the equivalent of up to 35,000 Nvidia GB300 chips. Data-centre debt issuance nearly doubled to about $182 billion in 2025, according to Morgan Stanley, showing how much of the build-out was already financed by borrowing.

2026.action_title: In 2026 to date, big-tech capex passed the 2025 total by September and every forecast was raised
paras: From January to September 2026, Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon and Meta spent about $508 billion on capital expenditure, more than in all of 2025, including about $207 billion in the third quarter. Their full-year guidance adds up to roughly $720–740 billion. Meta, Alphabet and Amazon spent more than their operations generated in cash, and between 26 October and 5 November Meta, Oracle and Alphabet raised more than $70 billion of new equity and debt. Oracle guided to $90–95 billion of gross capex for its fiscal year to May 2027. Amazon's nine-month total of $172.2 billion was larger than any company's full-year capex in 2025. Microsoft's third-quarter spending of $45.2 billion fell short of its own outlook of more than $50 billion because some third-party capacity was delayed, and Alphabet's free cash flow was about negative $9.1 billion in the quarter.

Forecasts rose throughout the year. Gartner's 2026 forecast for worldwide AI spending went from $2.52 trillion in January to $2.67 trillion on 16 September, up 49.5% on 2025. IDC's 2026 AI infrastructure forecast went from $487 billion to $521 billion after second-quarter spending of $121.4 billion. On these forecasts, AI spending will be about 42% of Gartner's $6.39 trillion of IT spending in 2026, by our calculation. IDC's second-quarter figure was up 53% on a year earlier, and servers made up 98% of its value. Gartner's September forecast split out spending on AI agents and assistants and raised its growth forecast for generative-AI models from 110% to 117%. Every forecast for 2026 made during the year was revised upward.

Menlo Ventures put US enterprise AI deployment spending at an annualised $176.8 billion in September, on a new definition, with Anthropic taking 55% of enterprise API spending. Gartner forecasts $29.2 billion for standalone AI agents and assistants. Public money stayed small: the UK launched a £500 million Sovereign AI Fund in April, Abu Dhabi's MGX closed a $49 billion fund in July, and Brookings counted $7.2 billion of US federal AI contract obligations by May. Menlo's figure is not comparable with its $37 billion for 2025. Google's share of enterprise API spending fell to 9% and OpenAI's rose to 31%. Gartner's broader $206.5 billion for 2026 counts all software with agentic features built in. A Futurum survey in September found 46.9% of enterprises over their AI budget in the second half, and Brookings' contract total was almost entirely defence.
